calls.reason: The Davis–Aaronson transcripts show one clear case: in problem 14, GPT-4 called the correct Wolfram result near zero. The second candidate was never checked, and the integral example involved tool errors, so 'a few cases' is not established.

Nobody independently replicated the authors' own observations. The Liu et al. citation audit shows search-tool flaws, but Kumar and Kats found that consensus answers solved every problem, so the evidence is mixed.

The experiment's own transcripts show protected-symbol errors that recur across problems 10, 11 and 26. In problem 26, seven Wolfram calls failed apparently over name conflicts and were never fixed, which fits 'often' and 'sometimes unable to correct'.

Independent results cut against the claim: Code Interpreter scored 92.9% on GSM8K, and Kumar and Kats gave it a solid passing grade. Neither tested Wolfram Alpha or simple science problems, and 'reliable' has no threshold, so the picture is unclear.
The only independent trace is one hemisphere-distance error from Kumar and Kats, which GPT-4 corrected when questioned. That is too thin to show a general commonsense gap in setting up word problems.

Valmeekam et al. (2023) found GPT-4 made valid Blocksworld plans only about 34% of the time, while 39 of 50 instructed humans succeeded. That is a clear gap against the modest claim that LLMs lack full human-level competence.
